```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)
```


## Problem 1
### Function
```{r p1_function}
bday_sim = function(n) {

  birthdays = sample(1:365, n, replace = TRUE)

  tibble(
    shared = as.numeric(length(unique(birthdays)) < n))
}
```
### Simulation

```{r p1_simulation}
bday_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000) |>
  mutate(
    estimate_df = map(group_size, bday_sim)) |>
  unnest(estimate_df) |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(prob_shared = mean(shared))
bday_results_df |> 
  filter(group_size %in% c(10, 20, 23, 30, 40, 50)) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

### Plot

```{r p1_plot}
bday_results_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob_shared)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path()
```
The probability that at least two people share a birthday increases with group size, and the increase is not linear. With 5 people the probability is `r bday_results_df |> filter(group_size == 5) |> pull(prob_shared)`. It first passes 0.5 at a group size of `r bday_results_df |> filter(prob_shared >= 0.5) |> pull(group_size) |> min()`, and with 50 people it is `r bday_results_df |> filter(group_size == 50) |> pull(prob_shared)`. The curve climbs fastest at moderate group sizes and then levels off near 1. A shared birthday becomes likely in fairly small groups because the number of pairs of people grows much faster than the number of people.
